title: Brazil Central Bank Declares Stablecoins Fuel Money Laundering
summary: A Central Bank of Brazil official commented that the institution was particularly concerned about the role of stablecoins in the remittance market, declaring that anyone who has good money and swaps to stablecoins knows it turns “bad,” linking these funds to money laundering. Central Bank of Brazil ...
content:
A Central Bank of Brazil official commented that the institution was particularly concerned about the role of stablecoins in the remittance market, declaring that anyone who has good money and swaps to stablecoins knows it turns “bad,” linking these funds to money laundering.

Key Takeaways

  • Brazil’s Central Bank declared that fiat to stablecoin swaps are consistent with money laundering.
  • This strict stance aims to ban fintechs from the remittance market and stop stablecoin sandwiching.
  • Authorities might further restrict stablecoin use by reviving a delayed 3.5% tax on crypto remittances.

Central Bank of Brazil Links Stablecoins to Money Laundering

The Central Bank of Brazil has linked stablecoin adoption to illicit activity, mentioning that exchanging fiat money for stablecoins characterizes money laundering.

According to reports from Livecoins, a local crypto outlet, a central bank officer reinforced the institution’s stance, highlighting that the bank was especially concerned about how these dollar-tied tokens were influencing the remittance market.

At a closed event attended by crypto company executives, Gerson Romantini, the Central Bank of Brazil’s Head of Exchange Division, remarked on the relationship between stablecoin exchanges and money laundering.

“Anyone with good money who goes into this stablecoin market knows their money has become bad. It’s not that it was bad at the origin, but the moment it transitions in this way, it starts to have a bad money mark, and from then on it is also characterized as money laundering,” Romantini declared.

The statement hints at an upcoming remittance ban on fintech companies, forcing them out of the market and leaving it exclusively to banks. An unidentified source quoted by Livecoins confirmed this idea.

Romantini also referred to a practice called stablecoin sandwiching, where these companies receive money in Brazilian reais, exchange it for stablecoins, and send it to another company abroad to pay bills or to intermediate family remittances. This is prohibited in Resolution No. 561/2026, issued by the central bank on April 30, 2026, effective on October 1, 2026.

Stablecoins have faced enormous pressure from regulators in Brazil, as users have been turning to these tools as a means of avoiding taxation while sending remittances and making cross-border payments.

The government has planned to tax these transactions since last year, with a 3.5% levy on all movements, including exemptions for users who don’t move over 10,000 Brazilian reais (nearly $1,910) monthly. Nonetheless, as the Lula Administration shifted into election mode, these plans were delayed because of their controversial nature, but they might resurface after his recent re-election.

The plan sparked a heated debate in Congress, with a crypto-linked faction vowing to fight the measure, arguing it would contradict national crypto regulation, which states that virtual assets are not national or foreign currency.

This is not the first time the bank has noted a connection between stablecoins and illicit activities. In February 2025, Gabriel Galípolo, President of the Central Bank of Brazil, stressed that people were using stablecoins because they are “buying things and don’t want to declare what they are buying because they want to avoid some type of taxation.”

title: JPMorgan Filing Shows Bigger Strategy Stake and $540 Million in Bitcoin ETF Shares
summary: A quarterly US securities filing has put fresh numbers around JPMorgan's exposure to crypto-linked investments. The filing shows larger reported positions in both Strategy, the Bitcoin treasury company, and BlackRock's spot Bitcoin ETF at the end of September. The figures are significant, but they n...
content:
A quarterly US securities filing has put fresh numbers around JPMorgan's exposure to crypto-linked investments. The filing shows larger reported positions in both Strategy, the Bitcoin treasury company, and BlackRock's spot Bitcoin ETF at the end of September. The figures are significant, but they need to be read with care: a Form 13F records reportable investment holdings at a particular date, not a continuous record of what a bank or its customers are buying today.

That nuance is especially important when headlines about large financial institutions are used as shorthand for bullish conviction. The disclosure tells us what was reported, but not necessarily who made each underlying investment decision or why.

The filing shows bigger positions in two familiar vehicles

The Block reported that JPMorgan's September 30 filing listed 848,932 Strategy shares, up from 624,387 in the previous quarter. The reported value was about $131.3 million. It also listed roughly 11.4 million shares of BlackRock's IBIT spot Bitcoin trust, with a quarter-end value around $540 million and a share-count increase of approximately 9.6%.

Those figures should not be mistaken for half a billion dollars of direct Bitcoin held in a wallet controlled by the bank. IBIT shares are securities that provide exposure through a fund structure. Strategy shares are equity in a company with a substantial Bitcoin treasury and its own operating and financing risks. Both can be influenced by Bitcoin, but neither is identical to owning a BTC coin on-chain.

A 13F is a snapshot, not a trading alert

Institutional investment managers disclose certain US-listed positions on Form 13F after a quarter ends. That means the most recent figures in this story reflect September 30 holdings, not positions on November 15. The filing does not show every asset or liability a reporting entity might have, and it cannot tell readers whether any listed shares were subsequently sold.

It also does not automatically establish that JPMorgan's own proprietary balance sheet made a particular directional bet. Reportable holdings may relate to investment management and other activities. Distinguishing those arrangements is essential before drawing conclusions about corporate strategy or client preferences.

Why the difference between Strategy and IBIT matters

Strategy provides a corporate route to Bitcoin exposure, but its share price also responds to debt issuance, financing terms, dilution and market expectations about its treasury model. NewsBTC's coverage of benchmark decisions involving Strategy and Metaplanet highlights a further variable: index rules can affect demand for company shares independently of the Bitcoin price itself.

An ETF operates differently. Fund shares seek to track the underlying Bitcoin exposure subject to fees and market mechanics, without conferring ownership of the issuer's broader business. An institution holding both securities might be accessing two different kinds of risk, or serving clients with different mandates. The filing alone does not reveal that motivation.

The market backdrop has changed since quarter-end

Bitcoin's price and the appetite for crypto products have deteriorated markedly since September. NewsBTC's reporting on November's spot ETF redemptions is a reminder that institutional positioning can change quickly. A larger September holding can coexist with substantial industry-wide outflows in November without either dataset being incorrect.

The sensible next step is to compare successive filings and separate share-count changes from valuation changes. Readers should also watch how managers describe their exposures, rather than attributing motives from the raw totals. This 13F offers useful evidence of institutional participation in crypto-linked securities. It is not a real-time endorsement of the current Bitcoin price.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Luxor CEO warns of AI ‘dark forest’ after Bitcoin miner hijack
summary: Attackers redirected customers’ Bitcoin mining power through Luxor’s Commander platform over the weekend, prompting its CEO to issue a warning to crypto businesses.
content:
Bitcoin mining services provider Luxor has warned that AI-enabled cyberattacks are becoming increasingly difficult to defend against after attackers compromised its mining-management platform and redirected customers’ computing power to another mining pool over the weekend. 

In an X post on Sunday, Luxor CEO Nick Hansen said the attack came through a “sophisticated AI-enabled vector,” without specifying how AI was used in the attack, warning that these types of attacks will only get more frequent over time. 

“At this moment, anyone running any sort of substantial business, especially in crypto, is inundated with AI-enabled attacks,” Hansen said in an X post. “This does not seem to be slowing down; rather, it’s speeding up as models get better and more attackers enter the arena.”

The warning comes as security researchers have documented the spread of AI-assisted hacking tools, raising the prospect of faster attacks against businesses holding money or controlling valuable infrastructure. 

“Abliterated models are running 24/7 against your entire surface, looking for a little crack, which they then use to (almost instantly) expand,” added Hansen. 

Hansen said Luxor has had to put the majority of its feature work on hold in order to harden its cybersecurity. The company has also acquired its own GPUs to run unrestricted open-weight AI models aimed at improving its security posture. 

“I urge anyone running a similar service to do the same.  It’s your only defense in this new AI-powered dark forest. ‘The only thing that stops a bad guy with a gun is a good guy with a gun.’” 

Bitcoin miners hijacked

Initial reports suggested that about 64,000 mining machines representing 13 exahashes per second were redirected to the OCEAN mining pool on Saturday. 

Luxor has not confirmed either figure, saying the incident affected just over a dozen customer accounts using its Commander mining-management tool. 

Luxor said it patched Commander within two hours of detecting the unauthorized changes and began restoring affected machines to their original pool settings. It pledged to compensate customers in full for the redirected mining power and publish a post-mortem.

Cointelegraph contacted Luxor for comment. 

Related: Coinone warns of phishing, identity theft after customer data breach

“We have explored the issue extensively, and it was isolated to the Commander tool. None of Luxor’s other services (including Luxor Pool and LuxOS) were affected,” said Luxor. 

Initial reports suggested the attackers received no mining rewards. However, a Bitcoin address identified by CoreX as associated with the incident subsequently received two OCEAN payouts totaling approximately 0.162 BTC, worth about $10,500. 

AI-assisted attacks on the rise 

Hansen’s warning follows a string of reported AI-assisted intrusions targeting crypto businesses. 

Earlier this month, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that a group called Crafty Falcon was using AI-powered tools to attack financial companies, including cryptocurrency exchanges, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis disclosed in October that an attacker used what it called “offensive agentic techniques” to access its systems. The breach exposed password hashes, live tokens and other customer information. 

Anthropic said in a September report that multiple groups had developed “automated exploit foundries” with AI, accelerating the pace of vulnerability research, testing, and exploit design.

title: Could Bitcoin Mining Use Scotland’s Stranded Wind Power? The Debate Is Heating Up
summary: Scotland produces substantial amounts of wind power, yet parts of that generation are sometimes curtailed because the electricity grid cannot move it to the places where demand exists. A new policy argument suggests Bitcoin miners could provide a flexible buyer for power that might otherwise go unus...
content:
Scotland produces substantial amounts of wind power, yet parts of that generation are sometimes curtailed because the electricity grid cannot move it to the places where demand exists. A new policy argument suggests Bitcoin miners could provide a flexible buyer for power that might otherwise go unused. The proposal is attracting attention because curtailment is expensive, but the economics are more complicated than simply turning spare electricity into digital coins.

The idea comes from industry advocates, not from an announced government programme. Whether it would reduce costs for consumers depends on location, grid rules, emissions and what miners would actually pay for the electricity.

Why wind power can be wasted despite strong demand

When transmission capacity is constrained, grid operators may pay generators to reduce output even when the wind is blowing. The system still has to maintain balance and ensure that power can reach customers safely. CoinDesk reported on an argument from the Bitcoin Policy Institute that flexible mining could help consume some of the energy affected by Scotland's network bottlenecks.

The reported cost of curtailment can exceed £1 billion a year, but that should not be mistaken for a pot of money miners could simply recover. Some payments arise from complex system constraints, and installing a new industrial load will not necessarily remove the need for other balancing actions. A credible proposal requires location-specific modelling rather than a national headline number.

What makes a mining operation flexible?

Bitcoin mining machines can, in principle, reduce consumption quickly when electricity becomes scarce or valuable elsewhere. They do not depend on uninterrupted processing in quite the same way as many conventional businesses. That gives miners a potential role as interruptible customers, willing to operate when power is cheap and switch off at times of peak demand.

But the equipment needs reliable commercial arrangements to justify its capital cost. A facility operating only during unpredictable periods of curtailment may earn too little to cover machines, buildings, cooling and maintenance. The central question is how many hours of usable electricity would be available and at what total delivered cost after grid charges and other expenses.

Climate and grid claims need separate evidence

Using energy that would otherwise be curtailed could be beneficial under certain conditions, yet it does not automatically make a mining site carbon-neutral. The actual comparison depends on the electricity mix, whether the new demand changes generator behaviour, the facility's operating schedule and the alternatives for the power. Grid reinforcement, batteries and other demand-response projects may compete to solve the same problem.

The broader mining sector is already weighing energy against new computing opportunities. NewsBTC recently covered MARA's Bitcoin sales and AI data-centre plans, while another report examined an AI-focused shift at Hyperscale Data. These moves show that miners are increasingly being judged as power and infrastructure operators as well as Bitcoin producers.

A workable pilot would answer hard questions first

Before declaring success, any Scottish mining proposal would need transparent figures for curtailment hours, transmission capacity, tariffs, environmental impacts and the ability to curtail the mine itself. It would also need to explain who captures the benefit: the miner, the generator, the network operator or bill payers. Those answers could support a limited trial, or show that another use of the electricity is better.

The debate is worthwhile because renewable generation and grid capacity are growing at different speeds. Bitcoin mining could be one tool in a larger flexibility toolkit. Presenting it as a guaranteed cure for Scotland's grid costs would be several steps ahead of the evidence.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Why Are Crypto Prices Down? Binance Founder CZ Lists Possible Reasons
summary: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao outlined possible pressures on crypto prices: IPO demand, fund withdrawals, security fears, inflation, and politics. He stressed that their relationship with the selloff remained uncertain while disclosing recent personal purchases. CZ Examines IPO Demand and Fund With...
content:
Binance founder Changpeng Zhao outlined possible pressures on crypto prices: IPO demand, fund withdrawals, security fears, inflation, and politics. He stressed that their relationship with the selloff remained uncertain while disclosing recent personal purchases.

Key Takeaways

  • CZ cited about $1.9 billion leaving U.S. bitcoin funds over seven sessions.
  • Binance committed more than $6.34 billion to cover hack losses.
  • CZ denied Binance sold crypto and disclosed buying during the decline.

CZ Examines IPO Demand and Fund Withdrawals

Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao, known as CZ, outlined potential reasons for the crypto selloff on X on Nov. 15, attempting to answer the question “Why are crypto prices down?” Noting that bitcoin’s low that day was $62,006, he stated:

“No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation.”

Bitcoin liquidations totaled $336.88 million over 24 hours as of 5:30 p.m. EST on Nov. 15, with long positions making up 50.2%, according to Coinglass. Across all tracked assets, liquidations reached $568.26 million over the same period, with 94,569 traders liquidated.

One possible pressure was money moving toward Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant. It launched its IPO roadshow on Nov. 10, beginning presentations to prospective investors. The proposed sale of 825 million shares at $70-$78 each could generate up to $64.35 billion before fees, combining shares offered by Anthropic and existing stockholders.

Binance Research examined AI financing concerns on Nov. 15, reporting bitcoin’s 15.6% decline over 11 days. Over the same period, perpetual contracts tracking AI cloud company Nebius (Nasdaq: NBIS) fell 27.5%. The team used those contracts as a proxy for sentiment toward businesses exposed to AI financing.

Fund withdrawals were another factor, with Zhao citing about $1.9 billion leaving U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds over seven sessions through Nov. 13, along with withdrawals from ether funds. Those consecutive sessions of bitcoin ETF outflows included approximately $1.07 billion during Nov. 9-13. Net outflows occur when redemptions, or withdrawals from a fund, exceed new investments.

Exchange Theft and Software Flaws Enter CZ’s Assessment

Security concerns included the Binance hack, drained iPhone-linked wallets, a Chrome exploit, and a Microsoft outage, which Zhao suggested could discourage crypto holdings. An exploit is code or a technique that takes advantage of a software vulnerability. For personal wallet protection, cold storage keeps private keys offline, reducing their exposure to online attacks.

The Binance theft was the subject of a Justice Department enforcement announcement on Nov. 12. U.S. authorities obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from the exchange. The department attributed the attack to North Korean hackers and reported that coordinated government and private-sector efforts had frozen more than $2.7 billion.

Separately, Binance said it had completed coverage of affected assets after committing more than $6.34 billion in company funds. The exchange also published a reserve snapshot covering 198 tokens, recording balances at midnight UTC on Nov. 12. That disclosure accompanied its update on replacing assets lost in the attack.

Inflation and US Policy Add to Crypto Uncertainty

U.S. inflation was Zhao’s fourth possible explanation, with hot readings raising expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase. Higher bond yields, the returns offered by bonds, can make interest-paying investments more attractive. A stronger dollar can also raise the cost of dollar-priced assets for buyers using other currencies, potentially weighing on cryptocurrency.

Political uncertainty completed his list, with the midterm results raising concerns about potentially stricter U.S. crypto policy. Beyond those potential pressures, Zhao addressed the exchange’s own activity during the downturn. He stated:

“No, Binance did not sell crypto.”

Turning to his own purchases, Zhao offered: “I bought crypto in the past few days, as I got some stablecoins recently. (maybe this is the cause)” as a joke about causing the selloff. He added: “Mid-long term, crypto will continue to grow.” The comments reflected his own views, he emphasized.

title: Three Central Banks Test a Bridge Between Traditional FX and Tokenized Settlement
summary: The Bank of England, Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank of Thailand have completed a cross-border foreign-exchange settlement experiment designed to connect existing payment infrastructure with tokenised systems. The project might sound technical, but it addresses a familiar financial problem:...
content:
The Bank of England, Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank of Thailand have completed a cross-border foreign-exchange settlement experiment designed to connect existing payment infrastructure with tokenised systems. The project might sound technical, but it addresses a familiar financial problem: two parties need to exchange different currencies without either being exposed to the risk that one side pays and the other does not.

The trial offers evidence that traditional central-bank settlement systems and distributed ledgers can be coordinated in a controlled setting. It does not mean a new public FX network has launched or that ordinary customers can use the prototype today.

The test focused on settlement risk

In their joint announcement, the three central banks described work under the Meridian FX APAC initiative. The experiment tested how payment-versus-payment settlement could function across different systems, including a distributed-ledger environment and conventional real-time gross settlement arrangements. Payment-versus-payment means one currency leg is settled only if the other can be settled too.

That principle is not new. What is new here is the attempt to apply it when separate technology stacks are involved. As the industry experiments with tokenised deposits and other digital representations of money, mismatches between systems can create delays or counterparty risks. A synchronised approach seeks to reduce that gap without requiring every participant to migrate onto the same ledger.

Netting could make the process less capital-intensive

The trial also explored multilateral netting. Rather than having every participant settle each obligation individually, a system can calculate offsetting positions so that fewer funds need to move. In principle, this reduces liquidity demands and can make cross-border payment arrangements more efficient. In practice, netting depends on legal finality, settlement windows and clear responsibilities if a participant fails.

Partior developed the prototype used in the trial, according to reporting on the project. This was a test environment, not a new production service from the central banks. Each jurisdiction's live payment systems and regulatory frameworks would still need to support any eventual deployment, which makes the operational path more complicated than a successful demonstration might suggest.

Tokenisation is only useful when money can actually move

Much of the industry's attention has been directed at tokenising bonds, shares or funds. Yet creating a digital security does not solve the equally important problem of settling the cash side of a transaction. If a tokenised asset settles instantly but payment remains trapped in an overnight banking process, a large part of the efficiency claim disappears.

That is why central-bank experiments deserve attention even from readers who do not trade foreign exchange. European work on tokenisation standards covered by NewsBTC reflects a related concern: interoperable rules and infrastructure are needed if digital securities are to operate beyond isolated pilots.

The timetable shows how far deployment still is

The Bank of England has discussed a synchronisation interface with a target timeline in 2028. That is a useful reminder of the gap between a promising proof of concept and regulated, always-available payment infrastructure. Security controls, access criteria and recovery procedures are as important as transaction speed.

For businesses, the near-term value is the direction of travel rather than an immediately available product. Stablecoin payment networks are already being used in commercial contexts, but central-bank settlement operates with distinct legal and systemic requirements. Meridian FX APAC shows institutions are working on the bridge between those worlds — carefully, and not yet at full scale.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Ripple’s David Schwartz Once Held 26 Million XRP. Now Just 3 Million
summary: David Schwartz revisited early crypto price doubts after disclosing substantial reductions in his XRP, bitcoin, and ether holdings. He attributed his sales to discomfort with investment risk while arguing that XRP would likely benefit from the ledger’s success. Schwartz Revisits Early Prices After R...
content:
David Schwartz revisited early crypto price doubts after disclosing substantial reductions in his XRP, bitcoin, and ether holdings. He attributed his sales to discomfort with investment risk while arguing that XRP would likely benefit from the ledger’s success.

Key Takeaways

  • Schwartz estimated his XRP balance was 88.5% below its peak.
  • He sold about 2.5 million XRP in 2025 and paid $1.7 million in taxes.
  • His remaining crypto included approximately 1 bitcoin and 6 ether.

Schwartz Revisits Early Prices After Revealing His Holdings

David Schwartz, Ripple’s chief technology officer emeritus and an XRP Ledger co-creator, revisited his early skepticism about crypto prices on Nov. 15. He stated on X:

“When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous. When BTC hit $200, that seemed ridiculous.”

His remarks followed a Nov. 10 disclosure that put his XRP holdings at approximately 3 million, down from a peak near 26 million. Those estimates represented an 88.5% reduction. His bitcoin and ether balances had also declined substantially from their peaks.

Detailing his XRP, bitcoin, and ether balances, the XRP Ledger co-creator wrote:

“It’s not a secret. I think I’m down from a high of around 26 million XRP to around 3 million XRP. Down from around 1,500 BTC to 1 BTC. Down from around 40,000 ETH to 6 ETH.”

During 2025, he sold about 2.5 million XRP, mostly received in 2020 and 2023, and paid approximately $1.7 million in capital gains tax. Those figures came from a separate Nov. 9 X post. Schwartz also said he received an IRS crypto tax reminder, which he described as a reminder to follow the law.

Sales Reflected Risk Tolerance Alongside Adoption Expectations

In a Nov. 9 explanation, he linked his sales to risk aversion, or discomfort with possible investment losses. Schwartz, who remained on Ripple’s board of directors, noted:

“I haven’t bought XRP in a long time. I am very uncomfortable with risk and have sold nearly all of the digital assets I’ve ever held. I still hold quite a bit of Ripple stock, and that alone is more risk than I wish I had.”

In a July 20 X post, Schwartz said he and his wife had agreed to sell at every new all-time high. Discussing his tolerance for investment risk, he expressed regret about those sales and wished he were more comfortable taking risks.

Alongside those personal decisions, his Nov. 9 comments expressed confidence that XRP would capture a substantial share of the value from successful ledger adoption. On Oct. 23, he called it very unlikely that the XRP Ledger would be highly successful in financial applications without high XRP demand and value, suggesting that outcome could require one completely dominant settlement asset, an asset used to complete payments between parties.

A video shared Oct. 28 showed Schwartz discussing his outlook for financial adoption at Swell, Ripple’s industry conference. He envisioned widespread use for managing money, receiving payments, investing, lending, and borrowing. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse described XRP’s institutional prospects while recognizing that fiat currencies and RLUSD suited some transactions.

Schwartz Explains What XRP Prices Suggest About Investor Expectations

On Jan. 29, Schwartz said he considered much higher XRP prices unlikely but would not rule them out. His own expectations had been wrong before: he once doubted XRP would reach 25 cents and began selling at 10 cents. Bitcoin at $100 had once seemed an impossible dream.

His example asked what would happen if many investors believed XRP had a 10% chance of reaching $100 within a few years. Those investors would buy XRP well below $10, absorbing cheaper supply and driving prices higher, he explained. In his view, XRP trading far below $10 suggested few investors believed strongly enough in that possibility to commit money, and he called claims otherwise untruthful. He added that the same math works for other prices, percentages, and time frames.

On April 30, Schwartz applied the same reasoning to wealthy investors who believed XRP had a 1% chance of reaching $10,000 within 10 years. He suggested those investors would buy XRP at prices up to at least $20, then asked why they were not doing so and whether a conspiracy explained it.

Both examples illustrated his personal view that crypto prices were generally rational. In his assessment, market prices reflected investors’ expectations about future prices and how likely those outcomes were. He also believed major bull runs often resulted from unpredictable external changes.

title: Kazakhstan Targets Tokenized Government Bonds After $22 Million Note Sale
summary: Kazakhstan wants to move from experiments with tokenised central-bank notes to government bonds recorded using blockchain infrastructure. Officials are targeting the first quarter of 2027 for a sovereign-debt issuance, following a transaction this month that placed about $22 million of central-bank ...
content:
Kazakhstan wants to move from experiments with tokenised central-bank notes to government bonds recorded using blockchain infrastructure. Officials are targeting the first quarter of 2027 for a sovereign-debt issuance, following a transaction this month that placed about $22 million of central-bank notes in tokenised form. It is a concrete development for the real-world-asset industry, although an important boundary remains: the government-bond deal is still a plan, not a completed sale.

That distinction is essential because tokenised securities announcements often mix prototypes, pilots and fully issued instruments. Kazakhstan has evidence of one completed step and an expressed ambition for the next.

The note sale provides an actual transaction to examine

As CoinDesk reported, the National Bank of Kazakhstan sold a total of 50 billion tenge in 91-day notes, with 10 billion tenge — approximately $22.3 million — issued through a tokenised arrangement. The notes carried a weighted-average yield of about 15.72%, and aggregate demand was roughly 1.4 times the offered amount.

Those details matter because they place the blockchain component within a recognisable debt-market transaction. Investors still care about the issuer, maturity, yield, settlement rules and custody. A digital token does not erase credit risk or replace the financial obligations underlying a security. It is a different technical representation and transfer mechanism for an instrument that remains subject to conventional legal and market questions.

Government bonds would be a distinct next step

National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov outlined an ambition to work with the country's Finance Ministry on tokenised sovereign bonds, with the first quarter of 2027 described as the likely timing. Central-bank notes and Finance Ministry bonds are not interchangeable: they have different issuers and may serve different investor or monetary-policy purposes. The future deal should therefore be assessed on its own terms.

The Kazakhstan Stock Exchange has said its digital-asset platform used Solana, with BitGo providing custody infrastructure, for the note initiative. It would be premature to conclude that those same providers are definitively selected for the government-bond transaction. Technical participation, permissions and investor eligibility need to be confirmed when official issuance documentation is available.

The benefits are practical rather than magical

Supporters of tokenisation point to shorter settlement cycles, clearer ownership records and the possibility of integrating securities with programmable workflows. Those benefits are plausible, but whether they materialise depends on legal recognition, interoperability with payment systems and the behaviour of market participants. A blockchain that records a bond is only one component of a working securities market.

For Kazakhstan, the experiment also sits alongside wider work on digital assets. NewsBTC previously reported on Kraken's in-principle regulatory approval in Kazakhstan, a separate initiative that highlights the country's interest in building financial infrastructure around the sector. Neither development means every planned crypto service has already received full authorisation.

What investors and institutions should look for

The next useful documents will set out who can buy the bonds, how transfers are restricted, which custodians are responsible for assets and how payments are settled. They should also explain whether investors can hold instruments outside a single controlled platform and how disputes would be resolved. Those are the details that distinguish a market-ready security from a demonstration.

The same questions apply to other tokenised securities projects integrating shareholder rights. Kazakhstan has moved beyond slides and into a completed note placement. The proposed government-bond issuance will be more convincing if it brings the same clarity about the legal and operational substance behind the token.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT
summary: Silicon Valley executives are reportedly organizing a campaign to bring Huang back and are looking to gain White House support.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 15, 2026

Silicon Valley executives are reportedly organizing a campaign to bring Huang back and are looking to gain White House support.

Jensen Huang is reportedly considering a return as Nvidia CEO just days after resigning from the company following reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to Nvidia, according to the Financial Times, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. One source told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for Nvidia’s chief’s return, and are looking to gain support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said.

Meanwhile, a public campaign called “Bring Jensen Back” has attracted more than 161,000 signatures, according to its organizers, who list Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its supporters. The campaign website also claims to have over 9,000 signatures from current and former Nvidia employees.

The push for his return goes against calls for new leadership at the AI chipmaker and coincides with an independent board investigation and scrutiny of its chip sales to China.

Related: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shake-up” of Nvidia’s leadership, urging the company to hire a CEO from outside the company, while US President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook take the job.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation following reports of alleged extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.

The controversy has also raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with US restrictions on AI chip sales, particularly involving customers in Asia with potential ties to China.

Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% on Thursday before recovering to close 4.3% lower, underscoring investor uncertainty over the AI chipmaker’s future leadership.

Cointelegraph reached out to Nvidia for comment.
